scope.end: 7a: 'a certain tenth, not an uncertain tenth', which proves that a priest who seizes a doubtful firstborn must return it (7a.1)

sections.title: The Garment Oath: A Deterrent, Even Against a Would-Be Thief?
sections.gist: R. Yochanan makes the oath a *takkanat chakhamim* against grabbing. The Gemara asks whether one suspected over money is also suspect on oaths and tests this against six oath rulings. Abaye then recasts the swearer as someone unsure whether he is owed an old loan.

children.title: R. Yochanan: A *Takkanat Chakhamim* Against Grabbing
children.gist: Each litigant ends up with the half he holds, so the oath has one purpose: a rabbinic enactment to stop people seizing others' garments.

bullets.text: Challenge: each stands holding half and walks away with the half he holds. Why is an oath needed at all?
R. Yochanan: the oath is a *takkanat chakhamim*, so that people won't go around seizing another's garment and saying "It is mine."
The oath here is not a way of finding out what happened. It is a deterrent: the prospect of having to swear should stop the grab, or make the grabber back down once he is in court.
This is the reverse of the question at the opening of the tractate, which asked why an oath is missing in some cases. Here the question is why one is imposed when the facts seem to settle the case.

children.title: *Migo De'chashid Amamona*: Is a Money-Cheat Also Suspect on Oaths?
children.gist: If the oath is aimed at a would-be thief, why trust his oath? The Gemara tests case after case, asking whether the swearer is a thief or only buying time. Three cases leave no such way out, and it concludes that suspicion over money does not carry over to oaths.

rows: *Modeh be'miktzat* (Torah)
Oath on the part he denies

Oath that the deposit is not in his possession
"I'm paying for it": people read *lo tachmod* as taking without payment

None given. Abaye: perhaps he is unsure whether he is owed an old loan

None given. Abaye: perhaps he is unsure whether he is owed an old loan

children.title: The Principle, and *Modeh Be'miktzat*: Buying Time, Not Stealing
children.gist: The Gemara holds that a money-cheat is not suspect on oaths. It tries to prove this from the Torah's oath for one who admits part of a claim, but that debtor may only be buying time.

bullets.text: Objection: *migo de'chashid amamona chashid ashvuata*. One suspected of taking money dishonestly should be suspect of swearing falsely too, so his oath is worthless.
Answer: we don't say this, since even one who steals treats a false oath as graver.
Proof: otherwise the Torah's oath for *modeh be'miktzat* (admitting part of a claim) would make no sense, since such a defendant is also lying about money.
The proof is rejected. Following Rabba, that debtor is only evading the creditor for a while (*ishtamutei ka mishtamit*): he intends to repay everything and admits part only to buy time.

Tosafot gives two reasons for the principle. First, a false oath is uniquely grave: the world shook at "You shall not take the name of the Lord in vain" (Yoma). Second, the oath reaches a person at a decision point, before he has committed to theft. That is unlike a proven *gazlan*, such as the shepherd on the previous daf, whom an oath can no longer stop.
The first reason reflects a troubling asymmetry: people are often far more careful about ritual matters than about other people's money.

children.title: Denying a Loan vs. Denying a Deposit: Who Loses Fitness to Testify?
children.gist: Rav Chisda: a refuted denial of a loan leaves one fit to testify, but a refuted denial of a deposit disqualifies. So why do bailees swear? They too may be buying time, unless witnesses saw the deposit in their house.

bullets.text: Rav Idi bar Avin in the name of Rav Chisda: one who denies a loan and is refuted by witnesses remains fit to testify. One who denies a deposit and is refuted is disqualified.
The reason: a loan is meant to be spent, so the denier is buying time. A deposit may not be used, so denying it is theft. This supports the distinction drawn for *modeh be'miktzat*.
Challenge from Rami bar Chama's baraita: all four bailees swear when they deny part of a claim and admit part. A bailee has no need to buy time, so why is his oath accepted?
Answer: he may be buying time too. If the deposit was stolen, he hopes to catch the thief and recover it. If it was lost, he hopes to find it in the marsh and bring it back.
Then why is one who denies a deposit disqualified? Only where witnesses testify that it was in his house, and he knew it, as he denied it (or he was holding it). Then he clearly meant to keep it.
The dividing line: an oath works on someone who is rationalizing. Once witnesses show that he knew exactly where the object was, no rationalization is left.

children.title: Rav Huna's Bailee Who Pays: 'I Gave Him Money' and *Lo Tachmod*
children.gist: A bailee who offers to pay still swears the deposit isn't with him. If he kept it, he can tell himself that paying makes it no wrong, since people read *lo tachmod* as taking without payment.

bullets.text: Rav Huna: a bailee who says the deposit was lost or stolen and offers to pay must still swear that it is not in his possession. If we suspect him of keeping it, why trust his oath?
Answer: even if he kept it, he can rationalize: "I gave him money for it, so I did nothing wrong."
Rav Acha of Difti to Ravina: taking another's property, even for payment, violates *lo tachmod* (Shemot 20:14).
Answer: people understand *lo tachmod* as taking without paying, so he may not realize he is sinning.
A person can break *lo tachmod* and still think of himself as honest because he is compensating the owner. That self-image is what keeps the oath effective.

children.title: Three Oaths With No Way Out: *Heset*, the Storekeeper, a Bailee's Three Oaths
children.gist: Three rulings impose oaths where no rationalization is offered, so the Gemara concludes: we do not say that one suspect over money is suspect on oaths.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman: one who denies a debt entirely takes a *shevuat heset*. If he is lying about money, why trust his oath?
R. Chiyya's baraita of the storekeeper and the laborers (3a): both swear and collect from the employer, although one of them is surely lying.

Rav Sheshet: an unpaid bailee who claims the deposit was stolen swears three oaths: that he was not negligent, that he did not misuse it, and that it is not in his possession. The court suspects him of theft, yet takes his oath.
Conclusion: we do not say *migo de'chashid amamona chashid ashvuata*.
In the storekeeper case there is little room for rationalizing: either he fed the workers or he didn't. The third of Rav Sheshet's oaths is the same: if the deposit is in his closet, he knows it.

children.title: Abaye: A Doubtful Old Loan, and Why People Fear a Doubtful Oath
children.gist: Abaye deflects the three rulings: the defendant may be unsure whether he is owed an old loan. Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi explains why such a person seizes money on a doubt but won't swear on one.

bullets.text: Abaye: there is no proof from the three rulings. Perhaps the defendant has an old loan he could never collect, and he is holding the plaintiff's property as repayment, not as theft.
Challenge: then he would swear as well, believing the property is his. The oath achieves nothing, so let him keep it without an oath.
Refinement: he is unsure whether the plaintiff owes him an old loan, and holds on to the property just in case.
Challenge: if he will seize property on a doubt, why won't he swear on the same doubt?
Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi: people shy away from a doubtful oath but not from doubtful money, because money can be returned and an oath cannot be retracted.

The gap between the two views is theoretical. The first holds that even a knowing thief fears a false oath. Abaye holds that people can almost always find some rationalization. Either way, oaths work in nearly every case.
The irreversibility of speech: people give themselves latitude with wrongs they think they can fix, and are careful with what can't be undone.

returns_to.note: Answers the three rulings that led to the conclusion

sections.title: R. Zeira: One Litigant Seizes the Garment in Court
sections.gist: R. Zeira asks about a litigant who grabs the whole garment before the court while the other is silent, then protests. Rav Nachman offers a baraita as proof, the Gemara deflects it twice, and the question stays open.

chart.caption: Rav Nachman's baraita: how each reading explains 'the one not holding must bring proof'
columns: Why the one not holding loses
rows: Rav Nachman's reading
Both held it; one seized it before the court
The seizer is now the one in possession
Yes: the seizer keeps it
Came back holding it
Told "go divide", they left and returned with one holding it
"You called him a robber, and then rented it to him without witnesses?"
No
Holding the edge
One holds the garment, the other only its edge
Holding the edge counts for nothing, even for Sumakhos
No

children.title: Silent, Then Shouting: Concession, or Relying on the Court?
children.gist: The question narrows to a litigant who was silent when the garment was seized and protested only later.

bullets.text: R. Zeira's question: both hold the garment, and one seizes it entirely from the other in the court's presence. What is the law?
If the other stays silent, his silence admits that the garment belongs to the seizer. If he shouts, what more could he do? Being stronger does not make the seizer the owner.

So the question is a man who was silent at first and shouted later. Did his silence concede, with the shout only later regret? Or does the shout show he kept quiet because the Rabbis of the court had seen the seizure?

children.title: Rav Nachman's Baraita: When One Holds It, the Other Must Prove
children.gist: A baraita limits splitting to when both hold the garment. Rav Nachman reads its other case as a seizure before the court.

bullets.text: Baraita: both swear and split only while both are holding the garment. If it is in one's possession, *hamotzi me'chavero alav ha'ra'ayah*: the one not holding must bring proof.
Read as stated, that is obvious. So it must mean that one seized it before the court, which is R. Zeira's case, and the seizer keeps it.
The implication would be surprising. In a dispute over a found object with no evidence either way, whoever happens to hold on longest in the struggle would become the possessor.

children.title: Two Deflections: Came Back Holding It, or Holding Only the Edge
children.gist: The baraita may describe litigants who returned from court with one holding the garment, or one holding it while the other grips only the edge. Neither reading speaks to R. Zeira's case.

bullets.text: Perhaps the court told them "Go divide it", they left, and one came back holding it. He says "He admitted to me"; the other says "I rented my half to him."
We tell the other: until now you called him a robber, and now you rented it to him without witnesses? So he bears the burden of proof, and there is no proof for a seizure before the court.
Alternatively, the baraita means what it says: one holds the garment itself and the other only hangs on to its edge.
Its point: even Sumakhos, who divides property of doubtful ownership without an oath, agrees that holding the edge counts for nothing.

sections.title: Consecrating the Disputed Property: Is a Declaration Like Seizing?
sections.gist: Can one litigant consecrate disputed property without seizing it? A bathhouse case prompts Rav Hamnuna's proof from doubtful firstborns, which Rabba rejects. Rav Chananya then proves from the animal tithe that a priest who seizes a doubtful firstborn must give it back.
sections.continues: Continues on 7a: Rav Acha of Difti asks which doubtful animals enter the pen, and the bathhouse is resolved by Rav Nachman's rule that property one cannot recover by law cannot be consecrated.

children.title: The Question: *Amirato Le'gavoah*, or 'His House in His Possession'?
children.gist: If a seizer keeps the garment, does consecrating it by declaration count as seizing, or must the thing be in one's possession to consecrate it?

bullets.text: R. Zeira's question is left unresolved, but the Gemara builds on it.
If the court takes the garment back from one who seizes it, then one litigant's consecration of the whole garment is void, since it isn't his.
If the court leaves it with the seizer, what if one consecrated it without seizing it?
Perhaps it works: *amirato le'gavoah ki'mesirato le'hedyot*, a declaration to the Most High is like handing over to a private person. So consecrating counts as seizing.
Or perhaps not: he never actually seized it. "When a man sanctifies his house" (Vayikra 27:14) teaches that, like his house, whatever one consecrates must be in his possession.

If consecrating counts as seizing, the other litigant's silence might be a concession, as it is when the garment is physically seized. If it doesn't, he has no need to answer words that cannot touch what he is holding.

returns_to.note: Builds on R. Zeira's unresolved question about seizing before the court

children.title: The Bathhouse Consecrated in the Middle of a Dispute
children.gist: One of two claimants consecrated a disputed bathhouse. The Rabbis stopped bathing there, and Rav Oshaya sent the question to Rav Chisda through Rabba.

bullets.text: Two men argued over a bathhouse that neither of them possessed, each saying "It is mine." One of them got up and consecrated it.
Rav Chananya, Rav Oshaya and all the Rabbis stopped bathing there, fearing they would misuse consecrated property.
Rav Oshaya asked Rabba to put the question to Rav Chisda in Kafrei. On the way, Rabba raised it with the Sages in Sura.
The claimant apparently consecrated it out of frustration at the deadlock.

children.title: Rav Hamnuna: The Priest Could Keep It, So It Is Already Sacred
children.gist: From Teharot 4:12 and a baraita, Rav Hamnuna argues that the priest's power to seize and keep a doubtful firstborn already makes it sacred. Likewise, the bathhouse consecration takes effect.

bullets.text: Rav Hamnuna cites Teharot 4:12. For doubtful firstborns (*safek bekhor*), human or animal, kosher or a donkey, *hamotzi me'chavero alav ha'ra'ayah*: the priest cannot take the animal, or the redemption money, from the owner.
A baraita adds that shearing and working such animals is forbidden, since they may be firstborns.
Rav Hamnuna reads the Mishnah as implying that if the priest seized the animal, the court would not take it from him.

Yet the animal is forbidden even when the priest hasn't seized it. So his ability to seize and keep it is enough to make it sacred, and in the same way the bathhouse consecration takes effect without seizing.

Examples of doubtful firstborns: a child born after a miscarriage when it is unclear whether forty days had passed since conception, or a calf when it is unknown whether the cow had given birth before.

Underneath is a question: in a case of objective doubt, does *hamotzi me'chavero* decide ownership, or does it only leave things where they are? If only the latter, a priest who grabs the animal is no thief, and the owner becomes the one who must prove.

children.title: Rabba: A Seizing Priest Must Return It; Sanctity That Comes by Itself
children.gist: Rabba: the court takes the animal back from the priest, and shearing is forbidden only because a firstborn's sanctity is intrinsic, not because of anyone's power to seize it.

bullets.text: Rabba: no proof. If a priest seizes a doubtful firstborn, the court takes it back, because seizing by force gives no right. The Mishnah means the priest must prove it is a firstborn.

Shearing and work are still forbidden because sanctity that comes by itself is different: a firstborn is sacred from birth, not by anyone's act, so the doubt about its sanctity is built into the animal.

Money and prohibition run on separate tracks. The animal is definitively the owner's under *hamotzi me'chavero*, yet it remains a doubtful firstborn. He may wait for a blemish, but he may not shear it or work it.

The open question is what the ruling means in a case of objective doubt: a real decision for the holder, or only a refusal to disturb the status quo. That question drives the tithe discussion that follows.

children.title: Rav Chananya: The Doubtful Animals Enter the Pen
children.gist: A baraita counts doubtful firstborns in the animal tithe. That would be impossible if a seizing priest could keep them, since the owner would be tithing with the priest's property.

bullets.text: Rav Chananya to Rabba: a baraita supports you. Doubtful firstborns enter the pen to be tithed with the other young animals for the animal tithe (*ma'aser behemah*), although a firstborn is not subject to it.
If a priest who seized such an animal could keep it, it might be his, and the owner would be exempting his own flock with the priest's property. Tithe must come from one's own animals.
The procedure: the animals born in a season pass one by one under the rod, and every tenth is sacred.
The shiur identifies these doubtful animals as lambs given to redeem a doubtful firstborn donkey. They belong to the priest only if the donkey really was a firstborn.

children.title: Abaye: Nine Plus One, Covered Either Way
children.gist: Abaye limits the baraita to an owner with nine animals plus the doubtful one, where either outcome is fine.

bullets.text: Abaye: no support for Rabba. The baraita is about an owner with only nine animals plus the doubtful one.
Either way it works. If it is not a firstborn, it is his, he has ten, and he tithes properly. If it is a firstborn, it belongs to the priests, and nine animals are not subject to tithe.
With eleven animals the argument fails. He would have ten without the doubtful one, and if it came out tenth, he would be tithing with what may be the priest's.

children.title: Abaye Retracts: The Jumping Sheep, *Minyan Ha'ra'uy*, a Certain Tenth
children.gist: A Mishnah exempts a whole pen when a counted animal jumps back in, which shows that only a certain tenth can be tithed. So the doubtful animals must definitely be the owner's, and a seizing priest must return them.

bullets.text: Abaye: what I said is wrong. A doubtful firstborn is not subject to tithe at all.
Proof from the Mishnah (Bekhorot 58b): if a counted animal jumps back into the pen among the uncounted ones, all in the pen are exempt.
If doubtful animals could be tithed, he should keep counting. Either this ten obligates him and he tithes properly, or one of them is the animal already counted and the other nine are exempt anyway.

They would be exempt by Rava's rule of *minyan ha'ra'uy*: a tally that was fit to reach ten exempts the animals counted in it, even if it was cut short, for example because one animal died and only nine remained.
Rather, the pen is exempt because "the tenth shall be sacred" (Vayikra 27:32) means a certain tenth, not an uncertain tenth.
The same applies here: a doubtful animal cannot be tithed. So the baraita that brings doubtful animals into the pen proves that a priest who seizes one must give it back.
So *hamotzi me'chavero* is a definitive ruling that the animal belongs to its owner, not a holding pattern, and the tithe rests on that real ownership.

children.continues: Continues on 7a: Rav Acha of Difti asks which doubtful animals the baraita means, since a doubtful firstborn is already sacred and cannot become tithe.

key_terms.sense: whether suspicion over money extends to oaths
key_terms.definition: The argument that a person suspected of dishonesty with money is, for that reason, also suspected of swearing falsely, so his oath should not be accepted. The Gemara's standard position is that this inference is not made.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara tests it against six oath rulings and concludes that it is not said, and Abaye explains the three hardest cases as a doubtful old loan.

key_terms.sense: a defendant who admits part of a claim
key_terms.definition: A defendant who admits part of the plaintiff's claim and denies the rest. By Torah law he must take an oath on the part he denies.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Offered as proof that a money-liar's oath is accepted, it is deflected: such a debtor is only buying time until he can pay.

key_terms.sense: burden of proof on the claimant
key_terms.definition: One who seeks to take property from another's possession bears the burden of proof. Without proof, the property stays with its holder.
key_terms.on_this_daf: It decides who must prove when one litigant holds the garment, and the Gemara asks whether, for a doubtful firstborn, it is a definitive ruling for the owner or only leaves the animal where it is.

key_terms.sense: verbal consecration as an act of acquisition
key_terms.definition: A verbal declaration consecrating property to the Temple is as effective as a formal act of transfer between private people.
key_terms.on_this_daf: It raises the possibility that consecrating a disputed garment counts as seizing it, against the requirement that what one consecrates be in his possession.

key_terms.sense: an animal or child whose firstborn status is uncertain
key_terms.definition: A child or animal that may or may not be a firstborn. Its owner keeps it unless the priest proves it is a firstborn, but the prohibitions of a firstborn still apply to it out of doubt.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Hamnuna uses it to argue that the power to seize suffices to consecrate. Rabba holds that its sanctity is intrinsic, and the tithe discussion proves that a priest who seizes one must return it.

key_terms.definition: The Torah obligation to pass one's newborn cattle and sheep under the rod each season and consecrate every tenth animal.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Whether doubtful animals may be counted in it shows whether a seizing priest keeps a doubtful firstborn, since only one's own animals, and a certain tenth, can be tithed.

key_terms.sense: a tally fit to reach ten
key_terms.definition: Animals counted for the tithe in a tally that could have reached ten are exempt from future tithing, even if the count was cut short before a tenth was designated.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rava's rule would seem to let the owner keep counting after an animal jumps back into the pen. That he may not shows that only a certain tenth counts.
aliases: a tally fit to reach ten

judgment_calls: Abaye's old-loan answer (s8) responds to the three rulings in s7 and could be nested under s3. It is kept as a sibling of s3 because it reframes the whole question of why the oath works; a returns_to link marks the connection.

The consecration question (s13) is framed conditionally on R. Zeira's question and could be nested under s9. It is made its own top-level section because it grows into a separate discussion (bathhouse, firstborns, tithe); s14 carries a returns_to link to s10.

The tithe discussion (s19) could stand as a top-level section on its own theme. It is kept under the consecration question because it serves only to support Rabba's premise in rejecting Rav Hamnuna's proof about the bathhouse.

Rav Chisda's loan/deposit distinction and Rami bar Chama's bailees are grouped in one subsection (s5), since the bailee challenge and the witness-disqualification answer turn on the same distinction; they could have been two sections.
7a.1 ('a certain tenth') is placed in s22 as the conclusion of Abaye's retraction, although the text does not name the speaker.
coverage_notes: The tallit-oath formulation (Rav Huna's 'I have a share in it') precedes 5b.8 and was covered at the end of the previous shiur; it is outside scope.
The essay places the opening question ('why is this oath necessary?') on 6a; the Sefaria text has it at 5b.8. Anchored to the text.
The essay describes Rav Nachman's shevuat heset case as a 'shomeret' who denies a debt; the text says one who denies a debt entirely. Followed the text.
The essay and segmentation apply Abaye's old-loan reasoning to someone grabbing the garment; the text has Abaye answering the three rulings (Rav Nachman, R. Chiyya, Rav Sheshet). Followed the text.
In the 'came back holding it' deflection, the essay has the other litigant say the holder agreed to buy his half; the text says 'I rented half of the garment to him.' Followed the text.
The essay names 'Rabbi Chanina' and 'Rabbi Oshaya' (bathhouse) and 'Rav Chanina' (tithe proof); the text has Rav Chananya and Rav Oshaya. Followed the text.

The essay and segmentation say the Teharot Mishnah rules that if the priest grabs the animal it is taken back; in the text Rav Hamnuna reads the Mishnah as implying the court does not remove it, and it is Rabba who says it is removed. Followed the text.
The essay attributes the 'priest's latent power sanctifies it' theory to 'the gemara'; the text attributes it to Rav Hamnuna. Followed the text.
The essay calls the tithe source a mishnah; the text has Rav Chananya citing a baraita. Followed the text.

The essay identifies the doubtful animals in the tithe pen as lambs redeeming a doubtful firstborn donkey; the in-scope text calls them doubtful firstborns, and the Gemara reaches the redemption-lamb identification only on 7a.2–3 (next daf). Kept as a shiur bullet.
The essay's 'parallel case' (moving the animal from one owner to another) is too vague to outline separately; its point is folded into the shiur bullet on money and prohibition as separate tracks.
